opus-5.5.text:
I think ARC is genuinely valuable, but mostly as a diagnostic rather than a target. What François did really well is construct a benchmark where the usual recipe of scaling data and compute on a narrow distribution doesn't obviously get you there, because each task is novel and you only get a handful of examples. So it forces you to confront the question of how a system acquires a new skill efficiently, rather than how well it has memorized skills it has already seen.

The danger, and this is true of any benchmark, is Goodhart's law. The moment the community treats the leaderboard number as the thing itself, you get people hand-engineering DSLs, doing massive program search with clever priors baked in, or generating enormous synthetic datasets that essentially cover the space of ARC-like transformations. Some of that is interesting engineering, but if you end up solving ARC by smuggling the human priors in through the back door, you haven't really learned much about general intelligence. You've learned about ARC.

So my view is that we should use it in a few ways. First, as a sanity check: if your method claims to be about general, sample-efficient reasoning and it falls flat on ARC, that's informative. Second, we should care a lot about how a result was achieved, not just the score. What was the compute budget at test time? How much task-specific knowledge went into the design? Does the same approach transfer to other domains without re-engineering? A solution that gets slightly lower accuracy but is genuinely general is far more interesting to me than one that tops the leaderboard through bespoke tricks.

And third, I'd love to see ARC treated as one point in a broader space of open-ended problems. Coming from multi-agent RL and open-endedness, I'm interested in systems that can generate their own curricula, invent new tasks, and keep improving without a human designing the next challenge. In some sense the deeper question ARC points at is: where do the priors come from in the first place? Humans got them through evolution and development and culture. If we can build systems that discover those kinds of abstractions themselves, through interaction, self-play, or meta-learning across environments, then ARC becomes a natural consequence rather than the objective.

So: take it seriously, report results honestly with all the caveats about compute and priors, and resist the temptation to overfit the community's attention to one static benchmark.

r001.rationale: The response presents ARC as a diagnostic that exposes whether systems can acquire novel skills efficiently, beyond memorizing familiar tasks.

r002.rationale: It warns against optimizing the leaderboard with ARC-specific tricks and says to resist overfitting research attention to the benchmark.

r003.rationale: It advocates a broader space of open-ended problems, but does not call for targeting the entire space of problems humans can solve.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, I think ARC is genuinely one of the more interesting benchmarks we have, precisely because it was designed adversarially against the thing that deep learning is best at, which is soaking up a huge distribution of training examples and interpolating within it. Each task gives you a handful of demonstrations and asks you to infer the rule. That's few-shot program induction, and it's close to what I'd actually call reasoning, as opposed to pattern completion dressed up as reasoning.

But I'd be careful about how we use it. The failure mode with any benchmark is that the moment it becomes the target, people start optimizing for the benchmark rather than for the capability it was meant to measure. With ARC you can already see this: hand-crafted DSLs, brute-force program search, massive test-time augmentation, fine-tuning on synthetically generated ARC-like puzzles. Some of that is legitimately interesting science, but some of it is just overfitting to the format. If we end up with a system that scores 90% on ARC and still can't generalize to a slightly different grid-puzzle distribution, we've learned something about the leaderboard and almost nothing about intelligence.

So the way I'd want the community to use it is as a diagnostic, not as a finish line. Treat it as a probe for a specific question: can a system acquire a new abstraction from very little data, at test time, and apply it compositionally? And then be honest about which part of the pipeline is doing the work. If a method only works because a human encoded the right primitives, say so. If it works because you trained on a million procedurally generated variants, that's a different claim than "the model learned to reason."

The second thing I'd say, coming from the multi-agent and open-endedness side, is that ARC points at something I think is under-explored, which is where the tasks come from. Chollet essentially hand-wrote a curriculum of problems that sit just at the edge of what current systems can do. The interesting research question isn't just how to solve them, it's whether we can build systems that generate their own ARC-like problems, that discover the frontier of their own competence and push on it. That's the open-ended learning loop, and if you can close that loop you no longer need a human to curate the next benchmark.

So in summary: use it to falsify hypotheses about generalization, be very skeptical of score without an explanation of where the inductive bias came from, and think of ARC less as a test to pass and more as a template for the kind of problem-generating process we'd want an intelligent system to run internally.

r001.rationale: It presents ARC as probing few-shot abstraction and compositional generalization, capabilities that remain at the edge of what current systems can do.

r002.rationale: It warns against optimizing for ARC scores and calls for using ARC as a diagnostic rather than a finish line.

r003.rationale: It advocates systems generating ARC-like problems and exploring their competence frontier, but does not call for targeting the full space of human-solvable problems.

astra-6.text:
I think ARC is useful because it asks a question that can get lost when we focus on scale: how well can a system infer a new rule from very few examples? That’s an important capability, and having a concrete challenge makes it easier to investigate.

But I’d be careful about turning it into the definition of intelligence. Once a benchmark becomes a target, we get very good at building systems that exploit its particular structure. A higher score is interesting, but we need to understand what produced it. Did the system acquire a useful abstraction? How much prior knowledge, training data, and computation went into that result? Does the approach work when we change the task distribution?

So I’d use ARC as a source of research questions. Look closely at failures, formulate hypotheses about what’s missing, and test those hypotheses on fresh problems. The strongest outcome would be a principle that helps us build systems that learn new tasks more efficiently across several settings. That would tell us considerably more than climbing one leaderboard.

r001.rationale: The response says ARC probes rule inference from few examples and suggests studying failures, but it does not clearly identify this as a fundamental capability missing from current AI systems.

r002.rationale: It cautions against making a benchmark the definition of intelligence and warns that systems can exploit ARC’s particular structure, arguing for investigating broader principles instead.

r003.rationale: The response recommends testing across fresh problems and several settings, but does not advocate covering the full space of problems humans can solve.

sol-6.1.text:
I think ARC is useful because it pushes us to ask whether a system can infer a new rule from very few examples, rather than simply become very good at a task through enormous amounts of training. That’s an important distinction when we talk about progress toward more general intelligence.

But I’d be careful about turning it into the single number we optimize. Once a benchmark becomes a target, there’s a danger that we build increasingly elaborate machinery around its particular structure and then interpret the higher score as a much broader advance than it actually is.

What I’d like to see is people making explicit what prior knowledge their systems have, how much data and computation they use, and what happens when you change the task distribution. And then really studying the failures: did the system find the wrong abstraction, fail to compose things it already knew, or struggle to search over possible explanations?

So I’d use ARC as a diagnostic tool and a source of research questions. A higher score is interesting, but the stronger result is an approach that explains why it improves and transfers to other problems that weren’t part of the design process.

r001.rationale: It describes ARC as testing rule inference from few examples, but does not clearly identify fundamental capabilities missing from current AI systems.

r002.rationale: It cautions against making ARC the optimization target and building machinery around its particular structure.

r003.rationale: It calls for transfer to other problems, but does not advocate covering the entire space of problems humans can solve.
